meta: Sarah Goodridge's miniature of Gilbert Stuart, painted in 1820 at his request and given by him to his mother.
about: A tiny oval miniature shows an elderly man in a dark coat and white cravat, attached to a braid of woven hair with a gold clasp. Gilbert Stuart asked Sarah Goodridge to paint it, because he believed nobody else could capture his personality. He called it the only true likeness of him. Stuart gave it to his mother, with a bracelet woven from his hair and his wife's. Family letters date the gift to 21 July 1827. Goodridge painted three miniatures of him, and this one was his favorite. |

meta: Kano Naonobu's Summer and Winter Landscapes, one of a pair of six-panel folding screens in ink on gold and silver ground.
about: Summer fills the right side of the pair and winter the left, in a sparse composition. A tiny boat drifts on the left. The Cleveland museum notes that the screens were once damaged. A later conservation added new sections of paper and inpainted them, aiming to keep the original flavor. Kano Naonobu was born in Kyoto, the younger brother of the painter Kano Tan'yū. In Kyoto he helped his brother paint for Nijō Castle. In 1630 the Tokugawa government called him to Edo. | https://openaccess-api.clevelandart.org
credit_line: Gift from the Collection of George Gund III

meta: Watanabe Shikō's pair of folding screens of flowers and trees of the four seasons, painted in ink, color, gold and silver.
about: Blossoming branches, iris, chrysanthemums and grasses crowd a pair of six-panel screens painted in ink and colour on a gold leaf ground. The Cleveland museum says Watanabe Shikō's interest in scientific realism grew out of dealings with his patron Konoe Iehiro. He joined careful drawing of plants to strong ink outlines and decoration in gold and silver. The museum calls the result an innovative style that influenced many of his peers in Kyoto. One plant in the screens is turmeric, called ukon in Japanese, which grows in Okinawa. | https://openaccess-api.clevelandart.org
credit_line: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund

meta: Apollonio di Giovanni's Adventures of Ulysses, a long tempera panel whose owners are traced from London in 1875 to Chicago.
about: Episodes of a sea voyage run along one long panel, from an island encounter through a palace, with gilded figures, swimmers and a ship of sailors. William Graham of London had owned it since at least 1875. A Christie's sale in 1886 listed it as The labours of Ulysses from a Cassone. Martin Colnaghi bought it there for 29 guineas. He acted for Francis George Baring, second Earl of Northbrook. The dealers Langton Douglas and Julius Böhler handled it later. Martin A. Ryerson of Chicago bought it from Böhler in 1911. | https://www.artic.edu/artworks/110760
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

meta: Francesco del Cossa's Saint Lucy, an altarpiece panel made for a Bologna family chapel and given to the National Gallery of Art.
about: Saint Lucy stands in a green mantle over a red dress and holds a dark palm frond. Floriano Griffoni commissioned the altarpiece for his family chapel in San Petronio, Bologna. Around the 1730s it moved to the Casa Aldrovandi in the city. Later Count Ugo Beni of Gubbio owned it, and a Beni sale catalogued it as a Saint Martin by Zoppo. A Berlin sale in 1929 called it Saint Liberalis. The Kress Foundation bought it in 1936 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1939. | https://github.com/NationalGalleryOfArt/opendata

meta: Fra Galgario's portrait of a young nobleman in a blue cap, probably painted as a private gift for a friend.
about: A young man in a red coat with gold embroidery and a loosely knotted white cravat looks straight out, wearing a dark blue cap with a gold tassel. The Walters Art Museum says the portrait has an informal, private character and was probably meant as a gift for a friend. The cap is the kind a nobleman put on at home when he was not wearing his wig. The painter Ghislandi was a lay brother of the Order of the Minims. His nickname Fra Galgario comes from a monastery in Bergamo. |

meta: Theodore Poulakis's Noah's Ark, in which Noah and his family watch animals enter the ark in pairs.
about: Noah and his family stand at the right, and the ark is at the left with animals entering in pairs. Birds fly toward it through the sky. God appears in clouds at the top and points to the ark with his right hand. A Greek inscription names the hand of Theodore Poulakis and describes Noah bringing his relatives and the animals into the ark. The painter copied an engraving by J. Sadeler. |

meta: Abraham Solomon's 1859 painting Not Guilty, in which a family greets a young man just acquitted in court.
about: A young man has just been acquitted, and his family crowds around him. His mother holds up one of his children, his wife embraces him, and his father thanks the lawyer at the right. Through an arched doorway in the background lies the open air, which the Getty reads as a sign of freedom. Abraham Solomon was very successful in his lifetime and worked in a major Victorian trend, genre pictures of contemporary life. He painted this one in 1859. |

meta: Jean-Baptiste Santerre's young woman with a love letter, sold in 1912 as a portrait of Charlotte Desmares and now in Boston.
about: A young woman with powdered hair and blue ostrich plumes looks aside, holding a folded letter in her right hand. She wears a black velvet bodice with red trim. At a Paris sale held by Madame Balletta in 1912, the painting was sold as a portrait of Charlotte Desmares by Santerre. It brought 6,000 francs from Charles Hour. Later that year Hour sold it to Delia Spencer Field, who lived in Paris and Washington. Her niece Catherine Spencer Eddy Beveridge inherited it and gave it to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston in 1947. |

meta: Robert Feke's portrait of Simon Pease, painted around 1749 for the sitter himself and later owned by the Corcoran Gallery.
about: A man in a brown coat with rows of buttons leans on a blue drape beside a stone column, wearing a powdered grey wig. The sitter, Simon Pease of Newport, commissioned the portrait from Robert Feke himself. It stayed in the Pease family until 1938, when it was sold to Albert Duveen in New York. Myron Charles Taylor owned it by the next year. The Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington bought it in 1965, and the National Gallery of Art acquired it in 2014. | https://github.com/NationalGalleryOfArt/opendata
credit_line: Corcoran Collection (Museum Purchase, Gallery Fund, William A. Clark Fund and Anna E. Clark Fund, 1965)

meta: François van Knibbergen's panoramic river landscape of 1655, bought by the Rijksmuseum at a Kampen sale.
about: A few figures stand on a small hill in the foreground, and far off a river carries many boats. François van Knibbergen signed the panoramic landscape at the lower right. It once belonged to Mrs Johanna Catharina Frederika Lemker of Kampen. At her sale in Kampen in 1908 it was catalogued as a panorama in the countryside around Cleves. The museum bought it for 1,000 guilders. | https://id.rijksmuseum.nl/20029294

meta: Ma Lin's album leaf of a scholar watching clouds rise, made as a response to a verse by Wang Wei written out by Emperor Lizong.
about: At the water's edge a scholar reclines beside a large rock, and the eye travels over an empty middle ground to a distant mountain. The Cleveland museum says the painting and a poem were once mounted together as one fan. Emperor Lizong wrote out a verse by Wang Wei about sitting to watch clouds rise where the water ends. Ma Lin answered it in this painting, using sparse ink and subtly graded washes. The museum sees it as a case of collaboration between an imperial patron and a court painter. Ma Lin was the son of Ma Yuan. | https://openaccess-api.clevelandart.org
